reference.source: Auerbach's Wilderness Medicine / Bove and Davis' Diving Medicine
clinicalPearls: An impairment of higher mental function caused by the anaesthetic effect of nitrogen breathed under increased pressure at depth
Onset and severity increase with depth; effects usually become noticeable at moderate depths and intensify progressively as the diver goes deeper
Symptoms resemble alcohol intoxication, with euphoria, impaired judgement and reasoning, slowed reactions, overconfidence, and reduced attention
The key feature is that it is fully and rapidly reversible on ascent to shallower depth, leaving no lasting deficit
The main danger is behavioural, as impaired judgement at depth can lead to fatal errors rather than direct physiological harm
Using helium-based breathing mixtures for deep dives reduces or avoids the narcotic effect
Prevention rests on limiting depth, careful dive planning, and adequate training and experience
reference.pathophysiology: Nitrogen narcosis reflects the anaesthetic action of inert gases dissolved in nervous tissue at raised partial pressure. As a diver descends, the partial pressure of the nitrogen in the breathing gas rises in proportion to depth, and the increasing amount of dissolved nitrogen interferes with neuronal signalling in a manner analogous to inhaled anaesthetics, producing dose-dependent central nervous system depression. Because the effect depends on the gas partial pressure and no structural injury occurs, it resolves promptly and completely once the diver ascends and the partial pressure falls.
additionalDifferentials: Early decompression illness affecting the nervous system
additionalInvestigations: Clinical recognition based on depth and the reversibility of symptoms on ascent
Review of the dive profile, depth reached, and breathing gas used
Assessment for other causes of impaired consciousness at depth (gas contamination, hypercapnia)
Analysis of the breathing gas mixture where contamination is suspected
Post-dive neurological assessment to confirm full recovery and exclude decompression illness
redFlags: Severe impairment at depth threatening safe diving behaviour
Failure of symptoms to resolve fully on ascent, suggesting an alternative diagnosis
Concurrent features of oxygen toxicity or gas contamination
Loss of consciousness or seizure while diving
reference.prognosis: Nitrogen narcosis is entirely reversible and leaves no residual deficit once the diver ascends; its significance lies in the risk of impaired judgement causing accidents at depth rather than any lasting physiological harm.
pitfalls: Underestimating impaired judgement and continuing to descend
Attributing narcosis symptoms to another cause and failing to ascend
Assuming tolerance develops, when susceptibility remains at depth
Overlooking coexisting hypercapnia or gas contamination that worsens narcosis
management: Manage acutely by controlled ascent to a shallower depth, which reverses symptoms fully and rapidly as the nitrogen partial pressure falls
Prevent recurrence by limiting maximum depth and planning conservative dive profiles
Use helium-based breathing mixtures (heliox or trimix) for deep dives to reduce or avoid the narcotic effect
Maintain a buddy system and dive supervision so that impaired judgement is recognised before it causes an accident
Exclude and assess other causes of impairment at depth, including breathing-gas contamination, hypercapnia and oxygen toxicity
Perform a post-dive neurological assessment to confirm full recovery and to exclude decompression illness
Reinforce diver training on the recognition and avoidance of narcosis
